text: Patents must be renewed annually to remain in force. Under Rule 80, renewal fees are due on the anniversary of the filing date, starting from the 2nd year. If renewal fee not paid, patent lapses (ceases to be in force). Renewal fees increase progressively — early years cheaper, later years more expensive. For AYUSH patentees: budget for 20 years of renewals, set calendar reminders, consider whether each patent still has commercial value before paying.

Patent renewal fees (e-filing) for natural persons/startups/small entities: Year 3-6: Rs 800/year, Year 7-10: Rs 2,400/year, Year 11-15: Rs 4,800/year, Year 16-20: Rs 8,000/year. For others (companies): Year 3-6: Rs 4,000/year, Year 7-10: Rs 12,000/year, Year 11-15: Rs 24,000/year, Year 16-20: Rs 40,000/year. Physical filing fees are ~10% higher. First 2 years fee included in filing fee. Late payment: additional fee applies.

If renewal not paid by due date: 1) Grace period — can pay with additional fee (Rule 80(1A)) within 6 months. 2) Lapsed patent — if still not paid, patent ceases. 3) Restoration — Section 60/61 allows restoration within 18 months of lapse if 'satisfied that failure was unintentional'. Restoration fee: Rs 2,400 (natural person) to Rs 4,800 (others) plus unpaid renewal fees. No restoration after 18 months — patent permanently lost. For AYUSH: always pay on time; restoration is uncertain and expensive.

Rule 80(3) allows paying renewal fees in advance for up to 4 years at a time. Advantages: 1) No need to track multiple deadlines. 2) Lock in current fee rates. 3) Simpler administration. Disadvantage: If patent becomes commercially useless and you want to abandon, can't get refund for advance payments. For AYUSH patents: consider advance payment for core patents likely to remain valuable; pay yearly for uncertain patents to maintain flexibility.

Renewal fees are due even while application is pending (before grant). Fees become due from the 2nd year after filing date. If you don't pay during prosecution, the application is deemed abandoned. Many applicants miss this — assume fees start only after grant. For AYUSH: if patent prosecution takes 3-5 years, you'll pay Years 2-5 renewal fees before even getting the grant. Factor this into patent budget.

Active portfolio management is essential: 1) Track all patents and applications with renewal dates. 2) Review portfolio annually — which patents still have commercial value? 3) Abandon patents that are no longer commercially useful rather than paying renewals. 4) Prune weak patents before expensive later-year fees. 5) Consider licensing underutilized patents to generate revenue. 6) Maintain renewal budget as a line item. For AYUSH companies: if a formulation was patented but never commercialized, abandonment may be better than paying Rs 40,000/year for Year 16-20.

When patents are assigned (sold) or transmitted (by operation of law, e.g., merger, death), ownership change must be recorded with Patent Office. Section 68-70, Rule 74: 1) File request for registration of assignment (Form 16). 2) Submit assignment deed/proof of transmission. 3) Pay fee (Rs 1,600 e-filing). 4) Controller records the change. Until recorded, assignee cannot enforce the patent against third parties. For AYUSH M&A: ensure all patent assignments are properly recorded post-deal.

If patentee's address or name changes, update records: File Form 20 with fee (Rs 500) to record change. Why important: 1) Official communications go to recorded address — missed communication can lead to missed deadlines. 2) Name discrepancy can cause problems in enforcement. For AYUSH companies: if you relocate, rebrand, or change legal entity name, update patent records promptly.

Patent expires at the end of 20 years from filing date. No extension possible in India. After expiry: 1) Invention enters public domain — anyone can use freely. 2) Renewal no longer required. 3) Patent number can still be referenced for historical purposes. 4) Trademarks may continue protecting the brand. For AYUSH: plan product lifecycle around patent term; consider follow-on patents for improvements; build brand value that survives patent expiry.

Deliberate abandonment of patent: 1) Simply stop paying renewal fees — patent lapses after grace period. 2) File Form 29 expressing intention to abandon (speeds up the process). Why abandon: no commercial value, litigation risk not worth the protection, defensive publication achieved, competitor's design-around made patent useless. Strategic consideration: abandoned patents become prior art — may still block competitors from patenting similar inventions. For AYUSH: abandoned formulation patents can still be valuable prior art.

If you have patents in multiple countries, maintenance costs multiply. Each country has its own renewal fee schedule and deadlines. Options: 1) Hire patent annuity service to manage payments. 2) Use IP management software to track deadlines. 3) Regularly review international portfolio — maintain only in commercially relevant countries. For AYUSH exporters: if you're not selling in Japan, consider abandoning the Japanese patent. Focus maintenance budget on key markets (India, US, EU, GCC countries).

Various changes require recordal with Patent Office: 1) Assignment — transfer of ownership. 2) License — recording optional but recommended (gives licensee standing to sue). 3) Mortgage/charge — patent as collateral. 4) Address/name change. 5) Legal representative after death. 6) Merger/demerger transmission. Forms: 16 (assignment), 17 (license), 20 (other changes). Fees: Rs 500-1600 depending on type. For AYUSH: keep Patent Office records current to avoid complications in enforcement or transactions.
